content: Many individuals undergo surgical procedures during their lifetime, which result in the creation of surgical wounds. After surgery, the incision is typically closed using methods such as sutures, staples, adhesive strips, or surgical glue. At the conclusion of the procedure, and before the patient leaves the operating room, the surgeon usually applies a wound dressing to cover the closed incision. This dressing may consist of gauze and adhesive tape or an adhesive pad designed to protect the wound. Currently, there is no standardized guidance on when it is safe to expose a surgical wound to water through bathing or showering after surgery. Early post-operative bathing may promote early mobilization of the patient, which is generally beneficial following most types of surgery. However, delaying bathing or showering for two to three days may lead to the accumulation of sweat and dirt on the body. On the other hand, early exposure of the surgical wound to water could potentially interfere with the healing process by causing irritation, maceration, or disruption of the wound environment. The objective of this review was to compare the potential benefits, such as improvements in quality of life, and the potential harms, such as an increased risk of wound-related complications, of early post-operative bathing or showering (within 48 hours after surgery, during the period of epithelialization) versus delayed bathing or showering (after 48 hours) in patients with closed surgical wounds. To address this question, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including The Cochrane Wounds Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL, DARE, Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid EMBASE, EBSCO CINAHL, the metaRegister of Controlled Trials, and the International Clinical Trials Registry Platform. The search was completed on June 30, 2015. The review included randomized controlled trials involving patients who had undergone any surgical procedure with closed surgical wounds, regardless of the wound's location or whether it was dressed. Trials involving patients with contaminated, dirty, or infected wounds, as well as those with open wounds, were excluded. Additionally, quasi-randomized trials, cohort studies, and case-control studies were not considered. Data were extracted on patient characteristics, risk of bias, and trial outcomes. For binary outcomes, risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated. For continuous outcomes, mean differences (MD) or standardized mean differences (SMD) with 95% CI were planned. For count data, rate ratios (RaR) with 95% CI were planned. All calculations were performed using RevMan 5 software. Only one randomized trial met the inclusion criteria for this review. This trial, which had a high risk of bias, involved 857 patients who underwent minor skin excision surgery in a primary care setting. The surgical wounds were closed with sutures. Patients were randomized into two groups: an early post-operative bathing group (n = 415), in which the dressing was removed after 12 hours and normal bathing resumed, and a delayed post-operative bathing group (n = 442), in which the dressing was retained for at least 48 hours before removal and resumption of normal bathing. The only outcome reported in this trial was the incidence of surgical site infections (SSIs). The results showed no statistically significant difference in the proportion of patients who developed SSIs between the early and delayed bathing groups. Specifically, 8.5% of patients in the early bathing group and 8.8% of patients in the delayed bathing group developed SSIs (RR 0.96; 95% CI 0.62 to 1.48). The authors concluded that there is currently no conclusive evidence from randomized trials to determine whether early or delayed post-operative bathing or showering has a significant impact on the prevention of wound complications. The wide confidence intervals around the point estimate mean that a clinically significant increase or decrease in SSIs with early bathing cannot be ruled out. The authors recommend conducting further randomized controlled trials to better evaluate the effects of early versus delayed post-operative bathing or showering.
